definition: A printed circuit board is a mechanically supported structure that uses patterned conductors, insulating materials, and mounted components to form an electronic circuit.
A schematic is a logical drawing that shows components and electrical connections without requiring their physical board positions.
Board layout is the physical arrangement of components, copper, holes, and mechanical features on a PCB.
A component instance is one placed occurrence of a catalog part with a stable identity such as R1, C1, or U1.
A reference designator is the short unique label, such as R1 or U3, used to identify one component instance.
A catalog ID is the stable internal identifier that links one part record to its symbol, footprint, models, properties, and mappings.
The manufacturer is the company identified as the producer of a specific electronic component.
A part number is the manufacturer-assigned identifier for a specific component or component variant.
A package is the physical body and terminal arrangement in which an electronic component is manufactured.
Pin count is the number of logical or physical terminals associated with a component package as defined by its authoritative data.
A function tag is a searchable label that describes what a catalog part can do without changing its primary component family.
A synonym is an alternate searchable name that resolves to the same catalog identity.
An authoritative source is a revisioned manufacturer, standards, or upstream engineering reference used to support a part property or model.
A revision is a version identifier that records exactly which source, symbol, footprint, model, or dataset was used.
Unknown data is information that has not been verified or supplied and must not be silently guessed to satisfy a design rule.
Tolerance is the allowed variation of a component value or design requirement from its nominal value.
Polarity identifies terminals or orientations that must be connected in the correct positive, negative, anode, cathode, or equivalent direction.
An orientation marker identifies the required rotational or pin-one reference for correctly placing a polarized or keyed component.
Mounting style describes how a component is physically attached to the board, such as surface mount or through hole.
Surface-mount technology attaches component terminals to pads on the outer surfaces of a PCB.
Through-hole technology mounts component leads through drilled board holes and solders them to plated pads.
